title: Hagar and Ishmael in the desert (Genesis 21:9–21)
hookLine: sent away with bread and water, Hagar weeps; God hears the boy and opens her eyes to a well

lines: BREAD AND A SKIN OF WATER.
cards: Isaac is born, the laughing baby.

When he's weaned, Abraham throws a great feast, and there Sarah sees Ishmael, Hagar's son, Isaac's older brother, laughing, or playing, or mocking: the Hebrew word shares a root with Isaac's name, and readers disagree about what it means here.

Sarah tells Abraham: send this servant and her son away. Abraham is deeply upset, the Torah says, because of his son. God tells him to listen to Sarah, and promises that Ishmael, too, will become a nation.
Early the next morning, Abraham takes bread and a skin of water, puts them on Hagar's shoulder, gives her the boy, and sends them away, into the wilderness of Beer-sheba.

teach.b: The water runs out. Hagar puts her son under a bush, walks off about a bowshot away, and sits down. In the old JPS translation: "Let me not look upon the death of the child."
She lifts up her voice and weeps.
Then a detail with enormous weight: "God heard the voice of the lad." Hagar is the one weeping, but it's the boy God hears.
His name, Ishmael, given by the angel before he was born, means God hears, and it comes true in the desert.
An angel calls to her: "What aileth thee, Hagar? fear not; for God hath heard the voice of the lad where he is." Where he is.
The Talmud reads those words as God judging him as he is right now, a thirsty boy, not by anything that might come later.
Then: "God opened her eyes, and she saw a well of water." The verse doesn't say God made a well. It says God opened her eyes.
The well was there all along; she was too deep in grief to see it. A midrash learns from this: all people are presumed blind until God opens their eyes.
She fills the skin, gives the boy a drink, and the Torah adds: God was with the lad, and he grew. This chapter is the synagogue Torah reading on the first day of Rosh Hashanah, the new year.
The year's reading includes a mother weeping in the desert, and a well she couldn't see.

games.q: you're Hagar. the water is gone and your son is dying of thirst. what do you do?
o: put him under a bush, sit a bowshot away, and weep.
games.why: she can't bear to watch him die, and weeps. God hears the boy, and opens her eyes to a well that was already there.

practice: Think of something that feels like a desert right now, a dry stretch, a place where you've run out, and let yourself admit it, the way Hagar sat down and wept.
Then gently look for a well you haven't noticed: a friend who offered help, a resource you forgot you had, a small thing keeping you going. Don't force it; if you pray, you can ask to see.
